title: The Chemist Who Sold Nirma From His Bicycle on the Way to Work
dek: In 1969 a 24-year-old government laboratory technician in Ahmedabad began making cheap detergent in his backyard and selling it as he cycled to work, without giving up his job.

story.event: Making detergent at home and selling it door to door while keeping a government job
story.summary: In 1969 Karsanbhai Patel, a 24-year-old chemistry graduate working as a laboratory technician for the Gujarat government, began making a phosphate-free detergent powder in his backyard in Ahmedabad and selling it door to door and on his cycle ride to work, at about Rs 3 a kilo with a money-back guarantee. He kept his job until the powder caught on, then set up shop; by 1985 Nirma had reportedly overtaken Hindustan Lever's Surf.
paragraphs: In 1969 Karsanbhai Patel was 24, the son of a north Gujarat farming family, with a chemistry degree and a job as a laboratory technician in the Gujarat government's geology and mining department in Ahmedabad. That year he began mixing a phosphate-free detergent powder in the backyard of his home, packing it himself and selling it as he cycled to work.

Washing powder was then a premium product in India. Hindustan Lever's Surf dominated, and most households still washed with bars of laundry soap. Patel priced his yellow powder at about Rs 3 a kilo. Nirma's own history sets that against Rs 13 for the cheapest brand on the market; Business Standard called it a third of the price of the cheapest popular detergent. He gave a money-back guarantee with every packet. He called it Nirma, after his daughter Nirupama, whose picture went on the pack; she died young, in an accident.

He did not give up his salary to do it. For a time Nirma was a one-man operation run alongside his day job, sold door to door and to people he met on the road. The low price depended on cutting costs everywhere: plain transparent packets, sometimes simply rolled and stapled, no printed box, and later a single line of distributors supplying shops directly. When the powder caught on in Ahmedabad, he left the government job and set up shop in the city.

In the early 1980s Nirma's jingle reached television, with a girl in a white frock twirling on the pack. By 1985, according to reports, it had overtaken Surf. Hindustan Lever answered with a plan it called Operation STING, for Strategy to Inhibit Nirma's Growth, and launched the cheaper Wheel in 1988, by which time Nirma reportedly held 60 per cent of the market. Rivals later undercut it in turn, and by 2014 its share was estimated at about 10 per cent.

quote.text: Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The Dhammapada's smith refines silver in small passes, from time to time, not in one great heat. Patel's first years had that rhythm: a few packets on the way to work, a salary kept, nothing staked on a single push. The verse is about refining oneself, which a slower pace can also leave room for.

reflection: It is easy to tell this as a story of daring, but most of what Patel did in 1969 was cautious. He kept his salary, made the product himself, sold it on a route he travelled anyway, and promised refunds so that strangers risked nothing by trying it. The bold part, the price, rested on all that caution.

You may feel that serious work demands one big leap. Sometimes it does. More often it looks like Patel's commute: a small amount each day, a promise you can afford to keep, and the patience to see whether people come back.
invitation: Think of one thing you are building and name the smallest version of it you could offer one person this week, with a promise you could keep if it disappointed them.

sources.title: Inventor of low-cost detergents (4 August 2010)
sources.supports: Born in 1945 into a north Gujarat farming family; BSc in chemistry; laboratory technician at New Cotton Mills, Ahmedabad, then with the Gujarat government's geology department; in 1969, aged 24, began making phosphate-free detergent powder in his backyard, named Nirma after his daughter Nirupama; kept his day job and sold the detergent while cycling to work; Rs 3 per kg, one-third the price of the cheapest popular detergent; money-back guarantee on every pack; a one-man operation in 1969; later set up shop in Ahmedabad; overtook Surf in the 1980s.

sources.title: 40 years ago...and now: Nirma girl endears, but brand's seen better days (5 November 2014)
sources.publisher: Business Standard (Sohini Das and Sayantani Kar)
sources.supports: Detergent a premium product, most households using laundry soap; Patel's door-to-door campaign in 1969 with rudimentary packaging; costs pared, including a single line of distributors supplying retailers directly, allowing Rs 3 per kg; the mascot was Patel's daughter and the name partly derived from Nirupama; an executive's statement that the girl on the pack is his late daughter, who died in an accident; by 1985 Nirma had overtaken Surf, according to reports; HUL's Operation STING and the launch of Wheel in 1988; Nirma reportedly 60% of the market by then; a market share of around 10% in 2014.

cross_checks.claim: In 1969, while employed as a laboratory technician, Patel began making detergent at home in Ahmedabad and selling it on his way to work and door to door.
He worked in the Gujarat government's geology (mining and geology) department.
Nirma sold at about Rs 3 a kilo, far below Surf.
The brand was named after his daughter Nirupama.
By 1985 Nirma had overtaken Surf, and Hindustan Lever launched Wheel in 1988 under Operation STING.

research_notes: No first-person interview with Karsanbhai Patel could be found, so the story states no thoughts or feelings and contains no quotations from him. Price: Business Standard (2010, 2014) and Nirma's own site give Rs 3 per kg; the Indian Express (2019) and Indian Television (2021) give Rs 3.50; the story says 'about Rs 3'. Comparison price: Nirma's site says the cheapest brand was Rs 13 per kg and the Indian Express and Indian Television give Surf at Rs 13, while Business Standard (2010) says Rs 3 was one-third of the cheapest popular detergent; both versions are given with attribution. Some secondary sources give Surf at Rs 15; not used. Daughter's name: Business Standard and Indian Television say Nirupama; the Indian Express says Nirmala; the story uses Nirupama. The timing of her death is not documented; the story says only that she later died young in an accident, as reported by Indian Television and an executive quoted anonymously by Business Standard. Employer: Business Standard says he was first at New Cotton Mills and later in the state geology department; others say the department of mining and geology; the story uses 'geology and mining department'. Start date: the Indian Express says Nirma emerged in the early seventies, against 1969 everywhere else; 1969 used. The date he left his job is not documented in reliable sources (a 1972 date circulates without a source), so none is given. Market share: '60 per cent' by 1988 is reported only with 'reportedly' (Business Standard 2014, 2016) or without a source (Indian Television), so it is attributed as reported; Business Standard put Nirma's share at around 10% in 2014 and 10-12% by 2015. Start-up capital is given variously as Rs 700 or a Rs 15,000 loan, only on low-quality sites, so it is left out. Funding is therefore 'bootstrapped' on the basis of a one-man backyard start while employed. Wikipedia's account of 15-20 packets a day over a 15 km ride has no cited source and is not used.
